Rashi on Eruvin 7b:1:1.english: In its entirety - A middle wall across its whole span.

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:1:2.english: And the courtyard was breached opposite it - [the breach was] less than ten [handbreadths wide].

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:1:3.hebrew: חצר מותרת - דלדידה לא הוי במלואה, ונשתיירו בה גיפופין מכאן ומכאן, לפיכך לגבי דידה פתחים נינהו, ולא אסרי עלה בני מבוי, שאין מבוי אוסר על חצירות הפתוחין לו, אבל חצירות אוסרין במבוי, שהרי דריסת רגליהם עליו, ורה"ר נמי לא אסר עלה, דחצר הפתוח לו כפתח הוא:
Rashi on Eruvin 7b:1:3.english: A permitted courtyard - Since in its case the enclosure was not complete, and partial partitions (gifufin) remained in it on either side, they are therefore considered openings with respect to it, and the residents of the alley do not prohibit it, since an alley does not prohibit courtyards that open onto it. But courtyards do prohibit the alley, since their feet tread upon it. And the public domain also does not prohibit it, since a courtyard that opens onto it is like a doorway:

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:1:4.hebrew: ומבוי אסור - קס"ד מדנקט, ונפרצה חצר כנגדו, משום דמיחזי כמבוי מפולש קא אסר ליה, ולאו משום דנפרץ לחצר. ורב יהודה מדנקט רחבה, אשמעינן דמשום מפולש לא מיתסר, וברחבה ליכא דיורין דליתסרו עליה; אבל אי הוה כלה לחצר, אסרי עליה. ולקמן מפרש טעמייהו, והיינו דקשיא דרב אדרב בתרתי: אי משום מפולש, אי משום הנפרץ לחצר, ואסרי עליה בני חצר, דנפרץ המבוי במלואו לרשות האסורה לו:
Rashi on Eruvin 7b:1:4.english: And the alley is forbidden - One might initially think that [Rav] phrased it as 'and a courtyard was breached opposite it' because it looks like a through-alley, so that he forbids it for that reason and not because it is breached into the courtyard. Rav Yehuda, however, phrased it as 'a wide open area,' to teach that because of a through-alley it is not forbidden, since in a wide open area there are no residents who would be forbidden on its account. But if [the alley] is entirely open into the courtyard, [the courtyard's residents] do forbid it. [The Gemara] explains their reasons later, and this is the difficulty: Rav against Rav on two counts, whether [the ruling is] because of a through-alley or because it is breached into the courtyard, such that the residents of the courtyard forbid it, since the alley is breached in its entirety into the domain forbidden to them.

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:2:1.english: I do not know - From whom did he learn it?

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:2:2.english: In Dura de-Ra'uta - A village of shepherds.

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:2:3.english: [An alley] that ends at its open area - and its open area was breached in the wall opposite it.

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:3:1.english: I will explain it to you - [This refers to] Rav's statement, which I learned from him.

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:3:2.english: Here they combined, here they did not combine - That is, this alley that Rav said is forbidden. There is a distinction in the matter: sometimes it is forbidden and sometimes it is permitted. If the residents of the courtyard combined with the residents of the alley, the residents of the alley are permitted. Rav's prohibition was not because the alley is open-through (mefulash), as will be established later in the case of “not opposite each other.” The courtyard case is cited for its novelty: even though the public enters through it and exits through it, it is nevertheless permitted, since the breach is less than ten amot, which counts as a doorway of a courtyard. But the prohibition on the alley is not because of a breach in the wall opposite it. Rather, the residents of the courtyard forbid it when they did not combine. For the alley, the breach is a full opening, so the residents of the courtyard forbid it, while it does not forbid them, as we said in the chapter “All the rooftops of the city” (later, Eruvin 92a), regarding a large courtyard breached into a small one. The residents of the large courtyard forbid the small one, i.e., they forbid it, because for them the small one is nullified to it, and the residents of the small one do not forbid the large one, because for the large one it is a doorway. Two courtyards with a doorway between them do not forbid each other, as we said in the chapter “Window” (Eruvin 76b): if the wall is breached up to ten amot, they may combine as two if they wish, or as one if they wish, since it is like a doorway, and both are permitted to each other.

Rashi on Eruvin 7b:4:1.hebrew: דרב אדרב נמי לא תיקשי - כלומר מהשתא מצינן למימר דרב יהודה בדורא דרעותא כרב עבדוה, כדאמרינן כאן שעירבו וכאן שלא עירבו, וברחבה ליכא דיורין למיסרי אמבוי:
Rashi on Eruvin 7b:4:1.english: Rav against Rav also should not be raised - That is to say: now we can say that Rav Yehuda in Dura de-Ra'uta (a place name) acted in accordance with Rav, as we said: here, where they made an eruv, and there, where they did not. And in an open public square there are no residents whose presence would forbid carrying in an ambuy (a recessed, alley-like space).

Tosafot on Eruvin 7b:1:1.hebrew: דאי דרב קשיא דרב אדרב בתרתי, דאמר רב: מבוי שנפרץ במלואו לחצר, ונפרצה חצר כנגדו, חצר מותרת - דבני מבוי לא אסרי עלה, דאין דריסתם עלה; ורשות הרבים נמי לא אסרה, דלא הוי פרצה יותר מעשר, והוי פתח. ומבוי אסור משום פילוש, דהעומד במבוי רואה רשות הרבים כנגדו ואינו רואה שיכול לנטות לכאן ולכאן. ומדנקט נפרצה חצר כנגדו, משמע דוקא שנפרצה חצר כנגדו אסור משום דהוי כמפולש; אבל אם לא נפרצה, אפילו אם לא עירבו מותר, אע"ג דנפרץ המבוי במלואו לחצר, משום דקסבר נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים, נידון משום לחי ופתח. ומתני' דגדולה מותרת וקטנה אסורה, מוקי לה בנכנסין כותלי קטנה לגדולה. וליכא למימר דאסור משום מפולש, ומשום שנפרץ במלואו ולא עירבו קאמר; דא"כ הוה ליה למינקט רחבה, דהוה משמע דאסור משום מפולש. וגם הוה משמע מדנקט רחבה ולא נקט חצר, מכלל דבחצר יש עוד איסור אחר, דהיינו משום שלא עירבו. אבל השתא דנקט חצר, משמע אפילו איסור דלא עירבו דשייך בחצר ליכא, אלא משום שנפרצה חצר כנגדו. והיינו דקשיא דרב אדרב בתרתי: דרב סבר נידון משום לחי ופתח ואסור משום מפולש, ורב יהודה סבר דאין אסור משום מפולש, ונראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים אינו נידון משום לחי ופתח. אסברא לך: כאן שעירבו, כלומר: רב לא אסר מטעם מפולש, ולא נקט נפרצה חצר כנגדו אלא משום שריותא דחצר, אע"ג דרבים נכנסין לה בזו ויוצאין לה בזו שריא. אבל מבוי אסור אפילו לא נפרצה חצר כנגדו, משום דנפרץ במלואו לחצר ולא עירבו, וסבר נראה מבחוץ אינו נידון משום לחי ופתח. ודווקא נפרץ במלואו; אבל אי לא הוה נפרץ במלואו שרי אע"ג דלא עירבו, כיון דאינה רגילה בו, כדאמר ונפרץ, משמע דאינה רגילה בו. והוא הדין דהוה מצי למינקט במבוי פתוח לחצר דאסור כיון דרגילה בו, אע"ג דלא הוי במלואו. אלא אי נקט הכי לא הוה קמ"ל רב מידי, דכיון דפתח גמור הוא, פשיטא דלא אתו רבים ומבטלי מחיצתא. אי נמי, לא הוה מצי למינקט בפתוח לחצר, דאע"ג דרגילה בו הוה שרי, הואיל ולבני חצר יש להם דרך לרה"ר בלא מבוי; דכגון זו כופין אותו על מדת סדום, כדאמרינן במי שהוציאוהו (לקמן עירובין ד' מט.) גבי חצר שבין שני מבואות:
Tosafot on Eruvin 7b:1:1.english: For if the difficulty is Rav against Rav on two counts, since Rav said: an alleyway that was breached in its entirety into a courtyard, and the courtyard was breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted - The residents of the alleyway do not prohibit the courtyard, since they do not tread upon it; and the public domain also does not prohibit it, since the breach is not more than ten [cubits] and counts as an opening. The alleyway is prohibited on account of pilush (lateral openness): one standing in the alleyway sees the public domain directly opposite him, and does not see that he can veer to one side or the other. From the fact that [Rav] specified that the courtyard was breached opposite it, it follows that only when the courtyard is breached opposite it is the alleyway prohibited, as it is then like an alley open on the side. But if the courtyard was not breached, it is permitted even if no eruv was made, even though the alleyway was breached in its entirety into the courtyard, because [Rav] holds that an alley that appears from the outside and is level on the inside is not judged by the rules of lechi and petach. As for the Mishnah, which says that the large alley is permitted and the small one is prohibited, we interpret it as referring to a case where the walls of the small alley enter into the large one. And one cannot say that it is prohibited on account of pilush, and that [the Tanna] is stating it because it was breached in its entirety and no eruv was made; for if so, he should have taught broad (rechavah), which would imply that it is prohibited on account of pilush. Moreover, from the fact that he said broad and did not say courtyard, it follows that a courtyard has another prohibition, namely that no eruv was made. But now that he said courtyard, it implies that the prohibition of no eruv, which applies to a courtyard, does not exist; the only prohibition is because the courtyard was breached opposite it. This is the difficulty of Rav against Rav on two counts: Rav holds that the alley is judged by the rules of lechi and petach and is prohibited on account of pilush, while Rav Yehuda holds that it is not prohibited on account of pilush, and that an alley that appears from the outside and is level on the inside is not judged by the rules of lechi and petach. Let me explain: here it is a case where they made an eruv. Rav did not prohibit on account of pilush, and he did not say the courtyard was breached opposite it except because of the courtyard's permitted status; even though people enter it from this side and leave from that side, it is permitted. But an alley is prohibited even if the courtyard was not breached opposite it, because it was breached in its entirety into the courtyard and no eruv was made, and [Rav] holds that an alley that appears from the outside is not judged by the rules of lechi and petach. This applies specifically if it was breached in its entirety; if it was not breached in its entirety, it is permitted even though no eruv was made, since people do not regularly use it, as the word 'breached' implies that it is not regularly used. The same would apply if he had taught the case of an alley open to the courtyard, which would be prohibited because it is regularly used, even though it is not breached in its entirety. But had he taught that, Rav would have taught nothing new, since it is a full opening and it is obvious that people will not come and nullify the partition. Alternatively, he could not have taught the case of an alley open to the courtyard, which would be permitted even though it is regularly used, since the residents of the courtyard have a way to the public domain without the alley. In a case like this, one compels him, on the measure of Sodom, as we say regarding one who was expelled (Eruvin 49a) with respect to a courtyard lying between two alleys:
